h1: Planning a beer pairing dinner menu course by course
title: Planning a Beer Pairing Dinner Menu | Craft Beer School
desc: How to plan a beer pairing dinner course by course, with Indian dishes, pour sizes, beer order and the pairing principles that make each match work.
teaser: Five courses, five beers and a table of friends. Here is how to build a pairing dinner where every match makes sense.
standfirst: A beer pairing dinner is a menu where each beer is chosen to lift a dish and each dish makes the beer taste better. Planning it is part cooking, part tasting and part pacing. Here is how to build one course by course.
sections:
Most good pairings use one of three ideas, which our guide to beer and food pairing basics covers in more depth.

  • Match intensity. Light dishes with light beers, rich dishes with fuller beers. A delicate fish needs a delicate beer.
  • Complement. Find shared flavours. Caramel malt with roasted or grilled food, citrusy hops with lime and coriander, roast with chocolate.
  • Contrast and cut. Carbonation and bitterness cut through fat and fried food. Acidity cuts richness, much as lime does.

Chilli heat needs care. Bitterness and high alcohol make spice feel hotter. A touch of malt sweetness and moderate alcohol calm it.
Plan the order like a flight

The menu should rise in intensity, just as a tasting flight does. Start with light, crisp, lower alcohol beers and finish with darker, stronger ones. A five-course dinner might run: pilsner or wheat beer, pale ale or saison, amber or brown ale, a porter or dunkel, then a stout or strong ale with dessert.

Keep pours small, around 100 to 150 ml per course. Offer water throughout. Five full pints over dinner is far too much. Smaller pours let guests taste every pairing and stay comfortable to the end.
A sample menu, course by course

Starter: Amritsari fish fry with a German pilsner or Kölsch. The crisp, carbonated beer cuts the batter. Its light malt does not overwhelm the fish. The carom seed in the batter and the beer's clean bitterness sit well together.

Second course: paneer tikka with a Belgian witbier or hefeweizen. Witbier's coriander and orange peel echo the spices and lime of the tikka. The wheat body stands up to the char without competing.

Main: Hyderabadi mutton biryani with an amber lager or English bitter. Toasty, caramel malt matches the browned onions and meat. Moderate bitterness refreshes without fighting the spice. Our guide to Indian food and beer pairing has more matches for regional dishes.

Cheese or savoury course: a mature cheddar or a smoked cheese with a brown ale or porter. Nutty, chocolate malt and a soft roast flatter aged cheese.

Dessert: gulab jamun or a chocolate dessert with a stout. A rich sweet stout or imperial stout matches the sweetness of the dessert. Roast balances the sugar. Our guide to beer and dessert pairing covers more options. The rule: the beer should be at least as sweet as the dessert, or it will taste thin and bitter.

Pairings that look good on paper sometimes clash. Make a small version of each dish a few days before and taste it with two or three candidate beers. Take a bite, then a sip, then another bite. Note which beer makes the dish taste better, not just which beer you like best on its own.

Watch for clashes: a very bitter IPA with a spicy dish can make it burn; a sour beer with a cream-based gravy can taste odd; a strong roast beer can flatten a delicate dish. If a pairing does not work, change the beer rather than the dish.

Serve each beer at its proper temperature. Lighter beers cold, around 4 to 7 °C. Ambers and browns a little warmer, around 8 to 12 °C. Stouts and strong ales warmer still. Bring the later beers out of the fridge in time.

Pour each beer just before its course arrives so it is fresh. Use small, stemmed glasses where you can, so aroma collects and guests can see the colour. Say a sentence about each pairing: why this beer goes with this dish. Then let guests decide whether they agree. Some of the best conversation at a pairing dinner comes from people who disagree.

Plan for guests who do not drink. Offer a non-alcoholic option for each course, such as a non-alcoholic beer, a kombucha or a spiced lemonade, chosen with the same care. Keep water on the table all evening.

Make sure everyone has a safe way home before the first pour. With good food, small pours and plenty of water, a pairing dinner should be a long, relaxed evening rather than a heavy one.

If the planning made you curious about why some flavours lift each other and others clash, that is sensory science. Learning to describe and predict those interactions is a skill you can train. It makes every pairing menu easier to design.
faqs: How much beer should I pour per course?
Around 100 to 150 ml per course is plenty. Smaller pours let guests taste every pairing without drinking too much.
An amber lager, English bitter or a malty pale ale often works well. Toasty malt matches browned onions and meat. Moderate bitterness refreshes without making the spice burn.
What beer pairs with Indian desserts?
A sweet stout or imperial stout pairs well with rich desserts like gulab jamun. The beer should be at least as sweet as the dessert.
